Which one would you choose if you were in my shoes? Any insights into team cultures, specific tech stacks in India, or remote-working fatigue at Atlassian would be highly appreciated!
Thanks in advance!

title: EPAM Systems Interview Experience | Campus Placement | Internship
content:
EPAM Systems visited our campus for the recruitment process, offering an internship opportunity and performance baseed PPO.

The selection process consisted of four rounds: Online Assessment, Group Discussion, Technical Interview, and HR Interview.

Here is my interview experience.

## Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an online assessment consisting of:

- 2 Medium-level DSA questions.
- MCQs covering technical concepts.

I would highly recommend **Striver's SDE Sheet** for DSA preparation. It is one of the best resources to build problem-solving skills and prepare for coding assessments.

I successfully cleared this round.

## Round 2: Group Discussion (GD)

After the OA, the EPAM team visited our college for the next stage of the recruitment process.

We had a Group Discussion round.

**Topic: How will you survive in a forest?**

We were given around 2–3 minutes to think about the topic and organize our thoughts. First, each candidate had to explain their individual approach, followed by the actual group discussion.

**My preparation tips:**
- Communication is the key in this round.
- Express your thoughts clearly and confidently.
- Listen to others and build on their points.
- Don't interrupt others or try to dominate the discussion.
- Focus on logical thinking and teamwork.

I cleared this round as well.

## Round 3: Technical Interview

This was the most important round of the selection process.

The interviewer started with DSA questions and then moved to core CS subjects and my projects.

**DSA Questions:**
1. Balanced Parentheses.
2. Detect a Loop in a Linked List.

Both questions were around Easy to Medium difficulty.

After DSA, the interviewer asked several questions from:

- Java: Core Java concepts and fundamentals.
- Spring Boot: Concepts and practical understanding.
- Projects: Detailed discussion about my projects and technical implementation.
- Operating Systems: Basic OS concepts.
- SQL: Queries and database fundamentals.


----

- **DSA:** Striver's SDE Sheet - https://takeuforward.org/dsa/strivers-a2z-sheet-learn-dsa-a-to-z (Best resource)
- **Java:** I went through around 100 questions from a Java interview preparation book - https://www.targettrek.in/book/java-interview-handbook
- **Operating Systems & SQL:** Love Babbar's YouTube channel.
- **Spring Boot:** Focus on Spring Boot fundamentals, annotations, dependency injection, REST APIs, and commonly asked interview questions.

Make sure you understand your projects thoroughly because interviewers can ask detailed questions about your implementation and technical decisions.

I successfully cleared this round.

## Round 4: HR Interview

This was the final round.

The HR interviewer started with my introduction and then asked:

1. Tell me about yourself.
2. Why do you want to join EPAM Systems?
3. Are you willing to relocate?
4. Are you comfortable working from the office five days a week?
6. A few other generic behavioural questions.

This round was relatively straightforward. Be honest, confident, and clear about your expectations and willingness to work according to company policies.

I cleared the HR round and successfully completed the selection process!

## Compensation Details

| Component | Compensation |
|---|---:|
| Internship Stipend | ₹27,500/month |
| Full-Time Fixed Salary | ₹8 LPA |
| Health Insurance | ₹48,000 |


Overall, it was a good learning experience. All the best to everyone preparing for EPAM Systems' campus recruitment! 🚀**Bold**

title: EPAM Systems Interview Experience (2025) | Selected 🎉
content:
First of all, I would like to thank the entire LeetCode community. Reading interview experiences shared by other candidates on LeetCode Discuss helped me a lot in improving my preparation and understanding real interview processes.

Now, I feel it's my turn to give back to this wonderful community by sharing my own interview experience. I hope this post helps someone preparing for EPAM Systems or similar companies.

- **YOE:** Fresher
- **College:** Tier 69
- **Graduation Year:** 2025
- **Company:** EPAM Systems
- **Role:** Jr Software Engineer
- **Package:** 8 LPA Fixed (60K per month in hand)
- **Application Platform:** Naukri (OFF Campus Opportunity)
- **Drive Location:** Hyderabad, India
- **Drive Date:** November 29, 2025
- **Final Result:** Selected ✅

## Application Process and Online Assessment

I applied to EPAM Systems through Naukri and received an online assessment on **November 25, 2025**.

The assessment consisted of:
- Aptitude questions.
- Two coding questions.

I was able to solve one of the two coding questions and was shortlisted for the recruitment drive.

## Round 1: Written Coding Test

**Candidates attending the drive:** Approximately 950

The first round at the recruitment drive was a written coding test.

### Problem Statement

We were given a list of pairs containing a string and an integer. We had to read the input, calculate the sum of integers associated with each string, and print the strings whose final sums were nonzero.

**Example:**

**Input:**
```text
Suresh 10
Suresh 20
Aditya 20
Aditya -20
```

**Output:**
```text
Suresh 30
```

**Explanation:**
- Suresh's total is `10 + 20 = 30`.
- Aditya's total is `20 + (-20) = 0`.
- Since Aditya's final sum is zero, we don't print Aditya.

### My Approach

I know this looks like a simple problem, but I wanted to demonstrate a good understanding of input handling and data structures.

- Created a `Pair` class to store the string and integer values.
- Used Java's `Scanner` class to read the input.
- Used a `HashMap` to calculate the sum associated with each string.
- Printed only those strings whose final sum was nonzero.

I wrote my solution on paper and submitted it for evaluation.

After evaluating the written tests, the recruiters shortlisted a few candidates for the next round.

## Round 2: Group Discussion (GD)

The topic for the group discussion was:

**"Impact of UPI on Rural Areas"**

There were 10 candidates in my group discussion panel, and only 5 were selected for the next round. Several panels were conducting group discussions simultaneously.

### My Contribution

I spoke about how UPI can help small shopkeepers and businesses in rural areas.

My points included:
- Shopkeepers can check their transaction history and account balance through UPI applications.
- Digital payment records can help them understand their sales.
- By analyzing sales patterns, shopkeepers can identify which products sell the most.
- They can use these insights to manage their inventory and restock products that are in high demand.

I was fortunate to be among the five candidates selected from my panel for the technical interview.

## Round 3: Technical Interview 1

After waiting for some time, I was invited for my first technical interview.

The interview was quite relaxed, and the interviewer appreciated the fact that I had solved **800+ problems on LeetCode**.

### Interview Questions

The interviewer asked me the following questions:

- Tell me about yourself.
- Solve **Valid Parentheses** (LeetCode problem).
- Implement binary search using recursion.
- What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
- How do you store images in an SQL database?
- What are alternative ways to store images?
- What is a REST API?
- Why did you choose MongoDB instead of SQL for your project?
- Explain the projects mentioned in your resume.
- Answer follow-up questions about Java and my projects.

### My Experience

I couldn't give a satisfactory answer to the question about storing images in SQL. The interviewer explained the correct approach to me.

He also asked several follow-up questions about my projects and the technologies I had used.

Overall, the interview went very well. I got the impression that I would be shortlisted for the next round.

### Feedback

The interviewer advised me to explore my projects and the technologies mentioned in my resume in greater depth.

**My takeaway:** Don't just build projects and add them to your resume. Be prepared to explain the architecture, design decisions, alternatives, and trade-offs involved.

## Round 4: Technical Interview 2

After the first technical interview, I was called for another technical round.

Interestingly, some candidates had only one technical interview, while others had two. At that time, I didn't know why.

After joining EPAM Systems, I met and asked my first technical interviewer about this. He explained that his level was lower, so he wasn't authorized to conduct the entire technical evaluation alone. That was why I had to attend a second technical round.

### Interview Questions

The interviewer asked me questions related to React.js, project architecture, JavaScript, and behavioral scenarios.

**React.js and Project Architecture:**

- Tell me about yourself.
- Draw and explain the architecture of your project.
- If data comes from the backend, how would you fetch and display it in React?(I wrote code for that in react but didnt used useeffect hook he said this component will rerender infinite times because i didn't used useEffect Hook)
- What is `useEffect` in React?
- What is the dependency array in `useEffect`?
- What happens if we remove the dependency array from `useEffect`?
- What happens if we call a state update inside `useEffect` without specifying a dependency array?
- Write React code to implement a counter with increment and decrement buttons.
- How do you pass data from a parent component to a child component?
- What are the different ways to share data between components in React?

**Behavioral and Situational Questions:**

- If another person on your team is performing better than you, how would you handle the situation?
- How would you maintain code quality in a project?
- How do you learn a new technology?
- How would you handle situations where a teammate performs better than expected?
- How would you contribute to maintaining quality and collaboration within a team?

The interviewer also asked approximately 8–10 leadership and behavioral questions.

### My Experience

When asked how I would fetch data from the backend and display it in React, I became nervous and forgot to use `useEffect` appropriately.

The interviewer pointed out that my implementation would cause repeated executions and asked me about the dependency array. I initially gave an incorrect answer about what happens when the dependency array is omitted, and he corrected me.

When asked how to pass data from a parent component to a child component, I answered Context API. He asked for other approaches, and I gave an answer that method uses store.js file. he said recoil

This round taught me that knowing a concept is different from being able to explain it clearly and apply it under interview pressure.

**My takeaway:** Revise React fundamentals thoroughly, especially hooks, state management, component communication, and the situations in which each approach is appropriate. Also, practice explaining your answers aloud instead of relying only on theoretical knowledge.

## Round 5: HR Interview

After the second technical interview, I had to wait quite a while before I was finally called for the HR interview.

### HR Interview Questions

- Tell me about yourself.
- Tell me about your family and background.
- Describe a feature that you are proud of in one of your projects.
- What are your achievements?
- What offers have you received?
- How many interviews have you attended so far?
- Why are you attending this interview when you are already working at Cognizant?
- Why do you want to join EPAM Systems?

### My Experience

I told the HR interviewer that I was working at Cognizant(I just joined there 10 days ago and i am in my training and during there is no notice period in cognizant and i can join immediatlely) in a testing role, but I was very interested in software development.

I explained why I wanted to move into development and tried to convince him that this opportunity aligned better with my career goals.

**An advice here, if you are working in a company and went for a fresher drive don't mention about your experience. if the HR guy felt that this job could be given to a jobless guy i may be doomed. luck may not be always your side.**

After the interview, the HR representative discussed my candidature with another person. I waited for around 10 minutes, after which they called me and informed me that **I was selected!**

## Final Result: Selected at EPAM Systems 🎉

At total they selected about 50 students that day and 40 students the next day from that location. greatful that i am in one of them. Currently i am working 

That moment was unforgettable.

After going through the online assessment, written coding test, group discussion, two technical interviews, and the HR interview, hearing that I had been selected made me incredibly happy.

Honestly, it was one of the happiest moments of my life. I felt a kind of happiness that I hadn't experienced before.

I am grateful to God and grateful to life for giving me this opportunity.
## Key Takeaways

I know even though how much talent you have there should be some luck involved for me to pass all these rounds i accept but without talent no luck can help you is what i can say.

Here are a few lessons I learned from this experience:

- **Practice DSA consistently:** Solving 800+ LeetCode problems helped me build confidence during the technical interview.
- **Don't underestimate simple coding questions:** Even straightforward problems can test your understanding of input handling, data structures, and problem-solving.
- **Prepare for written coding tests:** Practice writing complete solutions on paper without depending on an IDE.
- **Participate actively in group discussions:** Make relevant points, explain them clearly, and listen to other participants.
- **Know your projects thoroughly:** Be ready to explain the architecture, technologies, design decisions, and trade-offs.
- **Revise your fundamentals:** For a Java and React interview, make sure you understand core Java concepts, SQL, REST APIs, React hooks, state management, and component communication.
- **Practice behavioral questions:** Prepare genuine examples demonstrating teamwork, learning, accountability, handling failure, and maintaining code quality.
- **Stay calm during interviews:** Even if you make mistakes, listen to the interviewer, understand the feedback, and try to improve your answer.

## Final Words

I hope this interview experience helps candidates preparing for EPAM Systems and other software engineering roles.

Keep grinding one day you will see its results.

Thank you to everyone in the LeetCode community who shares their interview experiences. Your posts helped me prepare, and I hope mine helps someone else achieve their goals.

**All the best to everyone preparing for interviews! Keep learning, keep practising, and never give up.** 🚀

title: Rippling | SDE Intern + Performance-Based PPO | 44 LPA | Tier 2 College | Selected ✅
content:
Hi everyone! 👋

Recently, I got selected for **Rippling SDE Intern + Performance-Based PPO** through our on-campus placement drive. Sharing my interview experience and compensation.

**Offer Details:**
- Company: Rippling
- Role: SDE Intern + Performance-Based PPO
- College: Tier 2
- Location: Bangalore
- Internship Stipend: ₹1 Lakh/month
- FTE CTC: ₹44 LPA (₹36 LPA Base + ₹8 LPA Other Components)
- Result: Selected ✅

## Online Assessment (OA)

I received an email from our placement cell and applied for the opportunity. Next week, I received the OA link.

There were **3 DSA questions:**
1. Easy – String
2. Medium – Binary Search
3. Hard – Graph

Fortunately, I was able to solve all three questions.

After almost a week, our placement cell shared the list of shortlisted students, and luckily, I was one of them.

## Round 1 – DSA

**Question:** Design an in-memory Task Scheduler supporting task insertion, deletion, and execution based on priority.

**Follow-ups:** Handle tasks with equal priority, optimize time complexity, and discuss how the solution would work for millions of tasks.

I used Java and explained my approach, data structures, and time complexities. The interviewer was mainly focused on problem-solving and optimization.

## Round 2 – LLD

**Question: Design a Splitwise-like Expense Sharing System.**

The requirements were to add users, create groups, split expenses equally or by percentage, and track balances between users.

**Follow-ups:** How would you simplify debts between users? How would you make the design extensible for new split types?

I started with the basic classes and their relationships, then implemented the major functionalities in Java. We also discussed SOLID principles and design patterns.

## Round 3 – HLD + DSA + Managerial

**HLD: Design a Multi-Tenant Employee Leave Management System.**

The interviewer asked me to design a system where multiple companies could manage employees, leave policies, approval workflows, and leave balances.

**Follow-ups:** Database design, multi-tenant data isolation, caching, handling concurrent leave requests, and scaling the system.

**DSA:** One medium-level problem based on HashMap and Sliding Window.

**Projects:** The interviewer asked me to explain my college projects in detail, including the architecture, database selection, technical challenges, and my individual contributions.

**Java & Spring Boot:** A few questions on HashMap internals, multithreading, dependency injection, REST APIs, and Spring Boot annotations.

Since most of my experience was with Java and Spring Boot, the interviewer mentioned that **I would need to learn Python** for their tech stack. I said I was comfortable learning new technologies.

For the last **10 minutes**, we discussed Rippling's products, engineering culture, team collaboration, and what interns generally work on.

Overall, the discussion was quite interactive.

## Final Result 🎉

After completing all the rounds, I was eagerly waiting for the results.

Finally, our placement cell announced the selected students, and **I GOT SELECTED!** ❤️

It was definitely one of the happiest moments of my college life.

## Study Material 📚

Sharing some resources I followed during my preparation:

**DSA:**
- Striver SDE Sheet – https://takeuforward.org/prep-hub/strivers-a2z-dsa-sheet (Must follow)

**LLD:**
- Coding and concepts - https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL6W8uoQQ2c61X_9e6Net0WdYZidm7zooW&si=nSrk7EGDtJnfT9JE (Paid)


**HLD:**
-  TargetTrek HLD – https://targettrek.in/book/system-design/hld (Paid)
-  InterviewWithBunny - https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLPtUyMfD0mNJDZg50fg2CptjLBavHot47&si=4uMeiKoGH8LZDmc (but you'll need other resources for concepts)


**One more suggestion:** Always participate in LeetCode weekly and biweekly contests. They really help improve problem-solving speed, confidence, and the ability to perform under pressure.

## Final Thoughts ❤️

Coming from a Tier 2 college, I know how competitive placements can be.

My advice is simple: **Always stay prepared because you never know when an opportunity will come.** Practice DSA consistently and don't ignore LLD and HLD.



And most importantly, **believe in yourself and always have faith in God.** 🙏

All the best to everyone preparing for placements. Hope this experience helps someone! 🚀

title: Google FDE Onsite Interview | ₹95Lakhs CTC | Bombed the DSA Round!!
content:
You are given "N" cities. There are "M" roads - each of the "M" roads connects two different cities directly. 

When you go by a car from city 'x' to city 'y' via any one of the "M" roads - it costs you 1kg of fuel. 

Car starts from the 'source' city and goal of the car is to reach the 'destination' city. Initailly car have 'P' kgs of fuel. Some cities have re-fueling stations in them - whenever you visit a city which has re-fueling station in it - it is necessary to re-fuel your car to exactly 'P' kgs again. You are allowed to visit the same road multiple times. If you visit a road for 5 times - then it is counted as 5 times in the final answer as well. Source city will never be a station. 

Your task is to go from 'source' city to 'destination' city - 

1)First of all  prioritize the fact that in your path you should never reach negative fuel at any point of time. 

2)Secondly prioritize visiting minimum number of stations in the path. 

3)Thirdly prioritize using minimum number of direct roads in your path. 

Output {min_stations,min_roads} which you would have to go through to go from 'source' to 'destination' and if it is not possible to do - report that as well(as you might run out of fuel in the path)

**134 students** were shortlisted, including me.

It was a **direct interview conducted on campus**.

The questions were mainly based on:

- **Resume**
- **Projects**
- **Technical concepts**
- **Programming knowledge**

My key takeaway from this round:

> **Be prepared to explain everything you mention on your resume.**

If you have projects or technologies listed, make sure you understand their fundamentals and can explain your contribution clearly.

---

## **Round 2 — Company Office | ~8 Hours**

After the first round:

**134 → 33 candidates**

I was among the **33 candidates shortlisted** for the next stage.

The round was conducted at the company's **Lucknow office** and lasted around **8 hours**.

It consisted of multiple stages:

### **1. Technical Interview**

We had an individual technical interview with the company.

The discussion focused on technical knowledge, programming and the projects mentioned on the resume.

---

### **2. SQL Assessment**

We were given **10 SQL questions** to solve online.
5 easy & 5 were medium to hard level

So, if you're preparing for this role, make sure you're comfortable with:

- **Joins**
- **Subqueries**
- **GROUP BY**
- **HAVING**
- **Aggregate functions**
- **Window functions**
- **CTEs**
- **Basic query optimization**

---

### **3. DSA Assessment**

We were given **5 DSA questions** to solve online.

those 5 questions were:

1.  **prime or not**
2. **print pattern ABCD in pyramid form**
3. **searchinig in sorted array**
4. **paranthesis check**
5. **i forgot**
---

### **4. Explanation of Solutions**

This was one of the most important parts of the process.

After completing the SQL and DSA assessments, we had to **explain our solutions to the interviewers**.

We had to explain:

- **Our approach**
- **Logic behind the solution**
- **Why we chose that approach**
- **How the solution works**
- **Complexity where applicable**

This showed that the evaluation wasn't only about getting the correct answer.

> **You should be able to explain your solution, not just write it.**

---

# **Final Result**

Out of the **33 candidates**, only **2 candidates were selected** for the SDE role at Tranzita Systems.

Unfortunately, **I was not selected**.

**33 → 2 Selected**

title: Marsh McLennan | AI Native intern | India | Interview Experience & Process
content:
Sharing the recruitment process for the **Marsh / Marsh McLennan Global Services Software Engineering role**. The exact process can vary by campus, role and hiring batch, but this was the structure followed in my process.

DATED: 13th September
College: Tier 1.5
Fresher
on-Campus Drive
CTC: 15.4 (Joining bonus+TA+DA+ESOPS)

## Overall Process

The selection process consisted of:

1. **Round 1 – Online MCQ Assessment**
2. **Round 2 – Full-Stack Coding / Technical Assessment**
3. **Round 2.1 – Optional Coding/Technical Assessment**
4. **Final Interview Round**

There is an important point regarding the second and third rounds:

> If a third assessment is conducted, the better performance between Round 2 and Round 3 can be considered for the evaluation.

The cumulative evaluation includes the relevant assessment performance along with the **ATS/resume-based score and Round 1 performance**, after which shortlisted candidates move to the interview stage.

---

# Round 1 – Online MCQ Assessment

The first stage was an online objective assessment.

The questions focused primarily on basic technical knowledge, aptitude and logical reasoning rather than advanced DSA.

### Topics to prepare

* Programming fundamentals
* OOPs
* DBMS
* SQL
* Computer Networks
* Operating Systems
* Basic data structures
* Basic algorithms
* Logical reasoning
* Aptitude
* Pattern/series-based questions
* Basic output prediction

Based on candidate reports, the assessment can include logical aptitude, pattern recognition/missing-series questions and basic coding fundamentals.

For freshers, I would particularly recommend revising:

**OOPs → DBMS/SQL → OS → CN → Programming fundamentals → Aptitude**

---

# Round 2 – Full-Stack Coding / Technical Assessment

The second stage was a hands-on technical/full-stack coding round.

This round is more practical than Round 1. Candidates should be prepared to actually write and explain working code rather than simply answer MCQs.

Depending on the role, preparation should cover:

### Frontend

* HTML/CSS
* JavaScript
* React
* Components
* Props and state
* API integration
* Basic form handling
* Async/await
* HTTP methods
* Error handling

### Backend

* REST APIs
* Node.js / Java / relevant backend language
* Authentication basics
* CRUD operations
* API validation
* Exception handling
* Database connectivity

### Database

* SQL queries
* Joins
* GROUP BY / HAVING
* Subqueries
* Aggregations
* Normalization
* Primary/foreign keys
* Indexes
* Basic transactions

### Coding

Expect problems around:

* Arrays
* Strings
* Hashing
* Searching
* Sorting
* Linked lists
* Basic recursion
* Basic trees
* Time and space complexity

The emphasis can vary significantly depending on the specific Software Engineering opening.

---

# Round 2.1 – Optional Technical/Coding Round

A third technical/coding assessment may be conducted depending on the hiring process.

One important aspect of this process is that the third round is not necessarily an additional hurdle that simply gets added on top of Round 2.

The **better performance between the applicable Round 2 and Round 2.1 assessments can be considered** in the overall evaluation.

Therefore, if Round 2.1 is offered, it is worth treating it as another opportunity to demonstrate technical ability.

Preparation should be similar to Round 2:

* DSA
* Programming fundamentals
* Full-stack concepts
* SQL/DBMS
* OOP
* API development
* Debugging
* Problem solving

---

# Shortlisting / Composite Evaluation

After the assessment stages, the candidate's overall performance is considered.

The evaluation is not based only on one coding question or one interview.

The process can take into account:

* **ATS/resume-based score**
* **Round 1 MCQ performance**
* **Round 2 performance**
* **Round 2.1 performance, if conducted**
* Overall technical performance

The relevant/better coding assessment result is considered where the optional third round applies.

Candidates who clear the required threshold are then moved to the interview stage.

---

# Final Interview Round

This is where the process becomes much more discussion-oriented.

Based on recent Marsh McLennan candidate reports, technical interviews have included detailed discussion of the candidate's **previous experience/projects, programming concepts and technologies mentioned on the resume**. One August 2026 report describes a recruiter screening followed by two technical rounds, with questions around the candidate's framework, Java, OOP concepts and Selenium.

For fresher/software-engineering hiring, I would prepare the interview around the following areas.

## 1. Resume / Project Discussion

This is one of the most important areas.

Be prepared to explain every significant technology and project written on your resume.

Typical questions can include:

* Explain your project.
* What problem does it solve?
* Why did you choose this technology?
* Explain the architecture.
* What was your contribution?
* What challenges did you face?
* How did you debug the issue?
* Why did you choose SQL/NoSQL?
* How does the frontend communicate with the backend?
* How is authentication handled?
* How would you scale the application?
* What would you improve if you had more time?

A candidate report specifically mentions detailed discussion around the candidate's skills and projects, followed by Java/OOP and coding questions.

**Do not put anything on your resume that you cannot explain technically.**

---

# 2. Programming & DSA

The interview may include a coding/problem-solving component.

Topics worth preparing:

### Easy–Medium DSA

* Arrays
* Strings
* HashMap/HashSet
* Two pointers
* Sliding window
* Stack
* Queue
* Linked list
* Binary search
* Sorting
* Trees
* Recursion

You should also be able to explain:

* Brute-force approach
* Optimized approach
* Time complexity
* Space complexity
* Edge cases

Candidate reports for Marsh McLennan have included basic coding such as counting vowels in a string and asking the candidate to explain the approach, pseudocode and complexity.

---

# 3. OOPs

This is particularly important.

Prepare:

* Class vs object
* Encapsulation
* Abstraction
* Inheritance
* Polymorphism
* Method overloading
* Method overriding
* Interface vs abstract class
* Constructor
* Access modifiers
* SOLID principles
* Composition vs inheritance

Be prepared for both theoretical and code-based questions.

---

# 4. Java / Programming Language Fundamentals

If Java is listed in the job description or on your resume, prepare:

* JVM/JDK/JRE
* String vs StringBuilder/StringBuffer
* Collections
* ArrayList vs LinkedList
* HashMap
* HashSet
* Exception handling
* Checked vs unchecked exceptions
* Interfaces
* Abstract classes
* Multithreading basics
* Garbage collection
* Streams/lambdas

Recent Marsh McLennan interview reporting specifically mentions Java and OOP concepts.

---

# 5. SQL & DBMS

For a Software Engineer/full-stack role, I would strongly recommend preparing:

```text
INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY
Subqueries
CTEs
Window functions
Indexes
Normalization
ACID
Transactions
Primary/Foreign Keys
```

Typical interview questions can involve:

* Find the second/third highest salary.
* Find duplicate records.
* Explain different joins.
* Difference between WHERE and HAVING.
* What is an index?
* What happens internally when an SQL query executes?
* SQL vs NoSQL.
* Explain normalization.
* Explain ACID properties.

---

# 6. Full-Stack Concepts

Since the assessment is full-stack oriented, prepare the complete request flow:

```text
Browser
   ↓
React / Frontend
   ↓
HTTP Request
   ↓
REST API
   ↓
Backend / Server
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Response
   ↓
Frontend
```

You should be able to explain what happens at every stage.

Also prepare:

* REST
* GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE
* HTTP status codes
* JWT
* Authentication vs authorization
* CORS
* Middleware
* API validation
* Error handling
* Database connection pooling
* Basic caching
* Deployment fundamentals

---

# 7. Behavioural / HR Questions

The final portion can move toward behavioural and managerial questions.

Prepare answers for:

* Tell me about yourself.
* Explain your strongest project.
* What was your biggest technical challenge?
* Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
* Tell me about a difficult problem you solved.
* How do you handle deadlines?
* How do you work in a team?
* Why Marsh McLennan?
* Why should we hire you?
* Where do you see yourself in the next few years?
* What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Keep these answers based on **actual experiences**, preferably using the STAR structure:

**Situation → Task → Action → Result**

---

# What I Would Prepare for This Process

If I were preparing specifically for this hiring process, my priority order would be:

### Tier 1 — Must Know

* OOP
* SQL
* DBMS
* Java/programming fundamentals
* Arrays & Strings
* HashMap/HashSet
* Basic React
* REST APIs
* Project explanation

### Tier 2 — Important

* Linked List
* Stack/Queue
* Trees
* Searching/Sorting
* OS fundamentals
* Computer Networks
* Authentication/JWT
* HTTP
* Git

### Tier 3 — Good to Know

* System design fundamentals
* Caching
* Load balancing
* Microservices
* Docker
* Cloud fundamentals
* CI/CD

---

## Final Takeaway

The process appears to combine **objective technical screening + hands-on coding/full-stack assessment + resume/technical interview**.

The most important mistake to avoid is preparing only for LeetCode.

For this type of Marsh McLennan Software Engineering process, prepare across **three dimensions**:

**1. Aptitude + CS fundamentals**

**2. Hands-on full-stack coding**

**3. Resume/project + technical interview**

Recent candidate reports support this broader pattern: Marsh McLennan interviews have included project/experience discussions, Java/OOP, coding, logical reasoning and technology-specific questions, while current interview reporting also shows recruiter screening followed by technical rounds.

Because interview experiences vary by role and hiring batch, the exact questions and number of rounds should not be treated as fixed company-wide rules.

title: Blinkit SDE-1 Backend  | Off-Campus Interview Experience
content:
# I recently got selected for **Blinkit SDE-1 Backend** through an off-campus opportunity, and I wanted to share my interview experience along with the resources that helped me during my preparation.

Role: SDE-1 — Backend
Graduation: 2026
Experience: 6-month internship
Location: Gurgaon
Interview Process: 3 Rounds
Result: Selected 🎉

How it started

I received a call from Blinkit HR unexpectedly.

We had a brief conversation around my current work, notice period, location and previous experience. She mentioned that they liked my profile and wanted to schedule an interview.

The process consisted of three rounds:

DSA + Fundamentals → LLD/System Design → Cultural Fitment

Round 1 — DSA + CS Fundamentals

The first round was with an SDE-3.

We started with introductions and discussed some of the projects I had worked on.

Before jumping into DSA, the interviewer spent some time testing my understanding of CS fundamentals and backend concepts.

Some of the areas discussed were:

- What happens when a process creates a new thread?
- What is the difference between a process and a thread?
- How does context switching work?
- What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList internally?
- What is the difference between clustered and non-clustered indexes?
- When can an index actually hurt database performance?
- How does a database decide whether to use an index?
- What is the purpose of a composite index?

After the fundamentals discussion, we moved to coding.

# Problem 1 — Search in Rotated Sorted Array

I was asked to search for a target in a rotated sorted array.

I identified the modified binary search approach and explained how to determine which half of the array remains sorted.

We discussed the edge cases, implementation and complexity before moving to the next problem.

# Problem 2 — LRU Cache

The second problem was to design an LRU Cache with efficient get() and put() operations.

I discussed the combination of a HashMap and Doubly Linked List, explained why both were required and then walked through the implementation with a sample sequence of operations.

We also discussed the expected time complexity and some possible edge cases.

The interviewer seemed satisfied with the approach.

We ended the round with some discussion around the team and the kind of work I would be doing.

# Round 2 — LLD / System Design

The second round was with a Team Lead.

After introductions and a discussion about my experience, I was given a design problem.

Design a Food Delivery Order Tracking System

We used draw.io to work through the design and gradually built the system.

The round was more about design thinking and trade-offs than writing code.

Some of the areas we discussed included:

Order lifecycle
- API design
- Database schema
- Entity relationships
- Handling order-status updates
- Event-driven communication
- Kafka vs synchronous communication
- Handling high traffic
- Idempotency
- Failure scenarios
- Scalability
- Service boundaries

The interviewer kept digging into the reasoning behind each decision.

For example, if I chose an asynchronous approach, the discussion would move towards:

Why asynchronous? What problem does it solve? What happens if the consumer is down? How would you handle duplicate events?

I felt that there were a few places where I could have explained my design better, so personally I wasn't completely satisfied with this round.

However, I later received the HR call for the final round, so I was happy to know that I had cleared it. 😄

# Round 3 — Cultural Fitment

The final round was with the Manager.

This round was much more conversational.

We went through my resume in detail and discussed my previous experience, projects and technologies.

Some of the discussion revolved around:

- A challenging problem I had solved
- How I handled disagreements within a team
- A technical decision I made and its consequences
- How I prioritize tasks
- Things I learned during my internship
- Situations where I had to take ownership
- What I would like to work on going forward

The manager also asked follow-up questions based on my projects rather than simply going through standard behavioral questions.

The discussion lasted around 40 minutes.

At the end, the manager told me that he was happy with my performance and gave me the offer during the round itself. 🎉

Definitely one of the best interview moments I've had.

Final Result 🚀

Selected for Blinkit SDE-1 Backend!

Compensation
Base: ₹24 LPA
Performance Bonus: ₹5 L
1st Year Compensation: ₹29 L

I am a 2026 graduate with 6 months of internship experience.

Resources That Helped Me

A big thank you to all the platforms and creators whose content helped me throughout this preparation.

1. [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/) — My primary platform for DSA practice. Solved around 1600 problems and reached a peak rating of 2164.

2. [Codeforces](https://codeforces.com/) — Helped me improve problem-solving speed, implementation skills and algorithmic thinking. Solved around 800 problems with a peak rating of 1550.

3. [Inline Interview](https://inlineinterview.com/) — Helped me prepare specifically around my projects, internship experience and the kind of follow-up questions interviewers could ask.

4. [Striver](https://takeuforward.org/) — Helped me follow a structured DSA roadmap and systematically revise important patterns.

5. [TLE Eliminators](https://www.tle-eliminators.com/) — Useful for improving my algorithmic thinking and competitive programming fundamentals.

6. [Aryan Mittal](https://codewitharyan.com/) — Helped me prepare for LLD, especially around object-oriented design and approaching design problems.

7. [Gaurav Sen](https://www.youtube.com/@gkcs) — Helped me understand HLD and system design concepts and think about scalability and distributed systems.

8. [Engineering Digest](https://www.youtube.com/@EngineeringDigest) — Helped me strengthen my Java, and OOPS concept

Really grateful to everyone behind these resources for putting out quality content and making learning accessible. ❤️

A Few Takeaways

My biggest takeaway from the process was that backend interviews require more than just DSA.

You should be comfortable discussing the fundamentals behind the systems you build.

For SDE-1, I'd recommend having a solid understanding of:

DSA
OOP
OS fundamentals
Java internals
DBMS
LLD
Basic HLD

Also, know your resume inside out, prepare every singal question that could have been made from your resume, it really helped me a lot.

Anything you've mentioned can become a discussion point.

Don't just know what your project does. Know why you designed it that way, what alternatives existed, what went wrong, and how you would improve it at a larger scale.

That's my interview experience.

Hopefully, this helps someone preparing for their next interview.

Keep solving. Keep building. Keep learning

All the best!

title: Razorpay | SDE Intern | Aug 2025 [Offer]
content:
Background
Education: BTech CSE, 2026(passout), Tier - 3 college, India
Experience: In college(no prior experience)

Opportunity details
Date: Aug , 2025
Location: Bangalore , India
Role: SDE-1
Applied: Applied via college Training and Placement Cell

Interview Process

Round 1 - CV Shortlisting 
* Candidates who have a cgpa of 8+ got shortlisted for the OA round. At my time there were around 300+ people who were shortlisted.

After a week I got to know that the 1st round is scheduled.

Round 2- OA Process(90 minutes)
* There is three DSA quesstion (medium to hard) , I am able to solve 2 questions completely.
* There were 8 - 10 MCQ questions from the Database , MYSql , OS and Computer networks.

After the first round , I got the result that I am selected for next round. I have a time of one week to prepare for the interview.

Round 3 - Technical Interview(45 minutes)
* Started with the basic intro of mine, then interviewer introduced himself as well as with the round overview.
* One medium DSA question was asked from the Sliding window approach .
* I was able to find the brute force solution and then interviewer asked me to optimise it.
* I struggled a bit but then he gave me a hint so I figured out a way to optimise it and I optimised it but I missed an edge case of empty array then the interviwer corrected it with the test cases. Although he is happy that with hints I can properly solve the question and it impressed him a lot.
* 40 minutes were done , then he asked me about the ACID properties with examples which I explain and communicate with fintech examples. 
* At last, I asked what problems and technologies does the interviewer works on, and asked for feedback.In total, the interview went 8.5 - 9 / 10, according to me (based on the feedback the interviewer gave).

After round 3 , on the same day after 4 hours on the same day the HM interview is scheduled.

Round 4 - HM Interview(30-35 minutes)
* Started with the basic intro of mine, then interviewer introduced himself as well.
* Project discussion - 10 minutes of project discussion , interviewer really impressed with the project idea and its functionality.
* CV discussion - 15 minutes of CV discussion , we discussed about everything that is written in my CV including the tech stack like JS , topics were JWT , Bcrypy , authn , authz . We discussed about me as I was working as member of a tech club , my awards , my responsibility as member of the club.(even he checked my linkedin :) )
* AI discussion - 7-10 minutes of discussion about the basic AI models as I have worked as a freelance prompt engineer so digging on the basics of RAG and some LLM models how do you use and how do you appraoch.
* He also asked why do you wanna join the company , so he wants to know that as a college student how much I understand the company working or know what recent changes have done . (I prepared it well)
* At last, I asked what technologies does the company works on, and asked for feedback.In total, the interview went 9 - 9.5 / 10, according to me (based on the feedback the interviewer gave).

Result
I got selected and got the mail from TPC head the very next day and after 2 weeks of interview I got the offer letter and after 10 days I got the oppurtunity to travel to Bangalore to work with Razorpay.

Tips
1. Try to convey your strengths to the interviewer (DSA, projetcs, prior experience), so that the interview goes in that direction.
2. DSA problems asked in OAs are hard as compared to that which were asked in the interview. So anyone who cracks OA can easily crack the interview if thier communication and problem solving apprach is good.
3. Prepare your resume well. Read your prior experience and projects written in your resume, as they will see the keywords written and ask questions about them.
4. Be calm and try to listen to what the interviewer is saying as they'll drop hints that you need to pick up.

**Good Luck and All the Best!!**

title: Tide UK Fintech | SDE - 3 | Interview Experience | Offer Details | Java Backend
content:
Before getting into my experience at Tide, I want to share my interview experience, because the interview process itself was actually quite good and well structured.

**Offer Details**

Total YOE: 6 Years

Role Offered - SDE-3

CTC Offered: **₹40 LPA** — All Fixed

Employer PF Contribution: Maximum ₹1,800/month

ESOPs: 800


**My Interview Experience at Tide**
**Round 1 — HR / Initial Technical Discussion (30 Min)**

The first round was an approximately 30-minute HR call.

The interviewer asked some basic technical questions around:

Multithreading
Event-driven architecture
End-to-end project delivery

He also explained the role, responsibilities, and what I could expect from the position.

Overall, this was a straightforward discussion and a good introduction to the role.

**Round 2 — Code Review Round (60 Mins)**

The second round was a Code Review round, which I found quite interesting.

You are given roughly 50 lines of code, basically an API controller layer where almost everything is happening in the same place:

Service calls
Database calls
Event publishing
Business logic

The expectation is to identify problems and write at least 15 comments, including both major and minor issues.

Format

You get around 40 minutes to review the code and write your comments.

During this time:

Audio/video needs to be turned off.
You are expected to treat it like a real PR review you would do in your day-to-day engineering work.
Comments should be short and precise.
Ideally, one line or maximum two lines.
Around 10–15 words maximum per comment so the interviewer can quickly understand your point.

After that, there is another 20-minute discussion.

The interviewers mainly focus on the major issues you identified and ask questions like:

Why did you flag this?
What could be the impact?
What would you recommend instead?
What could happen in production if this isn't fixed?

The important thing here is not just identifying issues. You need to clearly explain the reason and potential outcome behind your comments.

The next day, I received feedback that I was selected for the next round, along with some additional feedback from the interviewer.

**Round 3 — Hiring Manager Round(60-75 Mins)**

The third round was with the Hiring Manager.

One Engineering Manager from the team I was being interviewed for joined the discussion.

The first 15–20 minutes were mainly about one of my projects.

You need to have strong end-to-end knowledge here because after understanding your project, the interviewer starts going deeper into your decisions.

Questions can revolve around:

Why did you choose this technology?
Why this architecture?
What alternatives did you consider?
What were the trade-offs?
What was your strategy?
How did you handle scalability?
What problems did you face?
What was your individual contribution?
How did you take the project from development to production?

So, if you're preparing for this round, don't just prepare your resume bullets. Know your project end-to-end.

Immediately after this round, HR contacted me and told me that I was selected. He also shared the feedback from the Hiring Manager.

Finally, I received the offer letter.

The ESOP structure was:

Approximate value at that time: £10 per ESOP
Total ESOPs: 800
Vesting period: 1-year cliff
After 1 year: 25% vesting = 200 ESOPs
From the 13th month onwards: remaining ESOPs vest monthly.

Personally, I didn't consider the ESOPs particularly valuable because the company isn't publicly listed, so there isn't a straightforward way to trade them like publicly traded shares.

For me, it felt more like paper money unless there is eventually a liquidity event.

The Only Perk I Really Valued
Remote Job

The biggest perk was definitely the remote work option.

However, ironically, I never really felt like I was working remotely.

There were days when I was sitting in front of my laptop for 12–14 hours.

So technically:

Remote job ✅

Remote lifestyle ❌ 😭
